courseTitle: NativeScript + Angular: Build Native iOS, Android & Web Apps

cues.en: To understand how navigation in a mobile app differs from navigation in a website or in a Web app,
we have to have a look at the different kinds of routing we have in a mobile app.
The most important concept you got to understand is that navigation in a mobile app typically works
in a stack.
So we have a stack based navigation.
Now, what does this mean?
It means that we have forward, backward navigation.
We push pages onto our stack of pages and then we pop them off to view the previous page.
And that essentially means that on a given page where we might have discontent, maybe does this a list
where we can tap one of these items and we are redirected to a new page and then typically we have this
back button or on Android we have the physical back button, which takes us back to the previous page.
Notice forward backward navigation is also something we see in the Web.
But one important concept, which is commonly applied in mobile apps is that pages are cached because
it really is like this well, stack of pages where it's not like I go to a new page, so dump the old
one instead.
The old one is kept and the new pages just pushed on top of it.
And you can think of this stack as well, being a stack of pages where you always view the topmost page.
So you always view the page at the top of the stack.
And therefore, if you push a new page on it, you see that page.
But if you don't pop that page, if you navigate back, you see the previous page.
But it's never destroyed.
It's just hidden by the page on top of it.
So to say dead will become important when we start passing data around and the life cycle of a page
becomes important for us.
We'll cover that in this module.
Now, forward, backward is very trivial, yet a very common way of navigating in mobile apps.
But a naver pattern, which we see a lot, is DTAP based navigation.
Now there we might have multiple page stacks at the same time, one stack living in each tab.
So on our page you might have tabs at the bottom which allow us to switch between different page stacks.
So different pages.
But then within each tab we might also be able to navigate forward and backward and that will be a separate
stack per tab.
It's also important to note that therefore you can mix and match these navigation concepts.
It's not like you have to ever have a list of items where you can go forward and backward or have tabs.
You typically have both where it's absolutely normal to have both.
Now, the last kind of navigation, though, it's not just limited to navigation, as you will see in
this course, is to have a site draw.
Well, there again, you could have multiple page stacks because a sidrah also allows you to switch
to a totally different stack of pages and then go back to that previous stack of pages you were in,
for example.
Now, as I mentioned, this is not just used for navigation.
And the core idea, of course, is that we typically have this menu icon in the top.
And when we pushed it, we opened a side door which could hold any kinds of actions we can execute that
could be links to other pages or stacks of pages, or that could just be a logout link, which redirects
us to the logout page, which I guess is also some kind of navigation.
So these are the three core concepts you got to keep in mind for the rest of this module.
And I will show you all three in this module in great detail so you will learn how to use tabs in your
native app.
You will learn how to use a side draw and you will learn how to go back and forth between pages, of
course.
But for that, let's have a brief look at what we're actually building in discourse so that you have
an understanding for which kind of navigation we need.
